unit.title: The well-ordered soul: happiness and harmony
unit.needIt: This helps you understand why it feels hard to stay focused on your goals. You can use these ideas to build better habits, like choosing to study instead of scrolling on your phone.
unit.why: The lecture explores how our inner selves can feel like a tug-of-war between different desires. It tells the story of how ancient thinkers tried to figure out how to make our minds work in harmony. By understanding these internal parts, we can learn to lead ourselves better.
unit.outcome: Apply ancient wisdom to improve your own self-regulation and focus.
unit.reachesYou: You feel this when you want to sleep in but know you need to get up for work. You also feel it when you try to stay off social media but find yourself clicking on apps anyway.
unit.do: Pick one goal you struggle to stick to this week. Create an external rule, like putting your phone in a different room, to help your 'reason' part win.

quiz.q: What did the students do to make a pre-commitment?
quiz.why: The lecture explains that writing it down turned a thought into a binding action.
quiz.quote: It became a pre-commitment because you wrote it down just thinking it didn't make a pre-commitment.

quiz.why: It is a physical tool used to create an external constraint on phone use.
quiz.quote: And the idea is that you take your cell phone and you put it in this little Ziploc bag, and while you're driving, you are unable to gain access to it.

quiz.q: What is the city-state analogy used for?
quiz.why: Socrates uses the city to help us understand the internal structure of a person.
quiz.quote: Socrates suggests at the end of the discussion in Book Two, which we read for last class, that the best way to understand what it is that's good for the tripartite human being is to think about what would be good for a city that is structured in the same way.

quiz.q: How does Plato define justice in relation to the body?
quiz.why: Plato argues that justice is the health of the soul.
quiz.quote: Roughly, justice is to the soul as health is to the body.

quiz.q: What does Plato say about the pleasure of self-regulation?
quiz.why: People who regulate themselves experience a higher form of pleasure.
quiz.quote: And those of us who have had the great pleasure of doing the second, says Plato, have recognized that that pleasure is a greater form of pleasure than the pleasure of Angry Birds.

quiz.why: It describes how we adapt to material goods and always want more to stay happy.
quiz.quote: The hedonic treadmill is the idea that in order to maintain the same amount of happiness, if it's based on material goods, requires us to run to stay in the same place.

quiz.q: What is the special function of a human being according to Aristotle?
quiz.why: Aristotle believes reason is what makes humans unique and good.
quiz.quote: Reason is, he writes at 1098, the special function of a human being.

crystal.key: A well-ordered soul uses reason to harmonize inner desires and achieve true happiness.

decoys.text: Happiness comes from having more material goods.
decoys.why: The lecture explains the hedonic treadmill, where more goods do not lead to more happiness.

decoys.text: Making a mental promise is enough to stay disciplined.
decoys.why: The lecture shows that many people need external constraints to stick to their commitments.

crystal.aha: When we use reason to balance our inner parts, we achieve a healthy and happy life.
